Poker / Beginner practice

Practice the next poker idea.

Learn one idea, see it worked through, then try a different example. This practice room supports the six-stage free poker course. Start with one skill; return for mixed practice after you have studied several.

There are six worked examples and 18 fixed questions, three per skill. Say your answer and reason before revealing the choices. Examples repeat after three mixed sets. These are fictional exercises in standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em, with enough counters for the stated actions. They teach mechanics and reasoning, not recommended betting lines.

Choose one idea to practice

Count the additional callFollow the action orderSeparate a made hand and a drawRebuild the best five on the riverSeparate facts and possible handsName the purpose of a bet

Each mixed set has one question per skill. There are three fixed sets, then the questions repeat. You can open an example when you need one.

Six skills, with one worked example and three questions each.

1. Count the additional call

Learn the idea and see a worked example

A call matches the current total wager. Subtract only what you already paid on this betting round. A payment on an earlier street does not pay a new bet.

Worked example: Blinds are 1/2. You posted the big blind of 2 and face a raise to 8 total.

Match 8 total after crediting the 2 already paid: 8 − 2 = 6 more. A raise to a total is different from adding that whole amount again.

Read the full stage explanation.

A blind already paid

Blinds are 1/2. You posted the big blind of 2. The button raises to 9 total. You have enough counters to call; no one else changes the wager.

How many additional counters does a call cost?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

A call adds 7, bringing your contribution on this round to 9. This counts the price; it does not decide whether calling is good.

A. Nine is the total you must reach. Your 2 on this round already pays part of it.

B. Adding the posted blind to the total counts the forced post twice.

C. Yes. The current total is 9 and you already paid 2 on this round: 9 − 2 = 7.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A raise after your bet

On the flop, you bet 5. Your one opponent raises to 17 total on this round. You have enough counters to call.

How many additional counters would a call add?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

The additional call is 17 − 5 = 12. Preflop contributions do not enter this subtraction. Choosing an action requires more than counting its price.

A. Seventeen is the opponent's total flop wager. Credit the 5 you already paid on the flop.

B. Yes. Match 17 after subtracting your 5 on this same round.

C. The raise is to 17 total, not by 17 on top of your bet of 5.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A new betting round

You paid 12 on the flop. On the turn, you have paid nothing yet and your opponent bets 6. You have enough counters to call.

How much does a turn call add now?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Start the contribution count again on each street: 6 − 0 = 6 more on the turn. The pot still includes earlier payments.

A. Yes. You have paid zero on the turn, so the full new bet of 6 is owed.

B. The flop payment stays in the pot. It is not a credit against a turn wager.

C. The earlier 12 is already paid. It is not added to the new call amount.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

2. Follow the action order

Learn the idea and see a worked example

At a six-player table, initial preflop action starts left of the big blind. After the flop, action starts with the first remaining player left of the button. A bet or raise can give a player another decision.

Worked example: At a six-player table, the first three players fold. The button is deciding. Both blinds remain.

After the button's initial action, the small blind and big blind still have initial decisions. Posting a forced blind did not use up their turns.

Read the full stage explanation.

Before the button

Six seats in initial preflop order are: first seat, next seat, cutoff, button, small blind, big blind. The first two fold. You are the cutoff.

After your initial action, which seats still have initial decisions?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

The button and both blinds still have initial decisions. This identifies the order without recommending a starting hand or an action.

A. The button also remains after the cutoff in this initial order.

B. Yes. All three seats follow the cutoff in the initial preflop order.

C. Folding removes those players from the hand. It does not remove the remaining players' decisions.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

Two players remain

This hand began with six players. After preflop action, only the button and big blind remain. The flop has just been dealt and nobody has acted on it.

Who acts first on the flop?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

The big blind acts before the button on this flop. Two remaining players in a hand do not change the original button to someone else.

A. Yes. Among the remaining players, the big blind is first clockwise after the button.

B. The button is last in the initial postflop order here. Preflop and postflop starting points differ.

C. Hand strength does not determine action order, and the private hands are not known to each other.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A player gets another decision

Only the big blind and button remain. On the flop, the big blind checks, the button bets 3, and the big blind raises to 9 total. Both have counters remaining.

Whose decision is next?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

The button has another decision. Calling, folding or making a legal raise can be available; checking does not match the new wager.

A. An earlier action does not settle a later unmatched raise.

B. The raise gives the other remaining player a decision before the raiser acts again.

C. Yes. The button must now respond to the big blind's unmatched raise.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

3. Separate a made hand and a draw

Learn the idea and see a worked example

Name the best hand you can make now. Then name a possible improvement separately. A flush needs five cards of one suit; four cards of that suit are not a completed flush.

Worked example: You hold T♥ 9♥. The flop is T♠ 6♥ 2♥.

Your private cards

T♥9♥

Shared board

T♠6♥2♥

The two tens make a pair. There are four hearts available, so you also have a heart-flush draw. Your pair exists now; the possible flush does not.

Read the full stage explanation.

Two features of one hand

These are your two private cards and the three shared flop cards.

Your private cards

Q♥J♥

Shared board

Q♠8♥3♥
Which description fits your cards now?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Your best five are Q-Q-J-8-3. The pair and the draw are separate facts. Neither establishes that you are ahead of an unknown opposing hand.

A. Yes. Your queen pairs the board's queen, and four hearts are available.

B. There are four hearts, not the five needed for a flush.

C. The two queens already form a pair, even though the hand can also improve.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A different flop

Use your two private cards with this flop.

Your private cards

A♣Q♣

Shared board

K♠9♣4♣
What do you have now?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Your current made-hand category is high card. A possible club on a later street could improve it, but a draw is not a made flush or a guaranteed winner.

A. Only one ace is available to you. A high private card is not a pair by itself.

B. Your two clubs plus two on the board make four clubs, not five.

C. Yes. The five ranks are all different, and four clubs are available.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A paired starting hand

Use your two private cards with this flop.

Your private cards

8♠8♦

Shared board

K♥8♣2♥
Which made hand can you build?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Three of a kind is available now. The king is a kicker, not a reason to discard the matching eight on the board.

A. Count the board's eight as well as your two private eights.

B. Yes. Your two eights and the board's eight make three of a kind.

C. Only two hearts are available, both on the board. Five are required.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

4. Rebuild the best five on the river

Learn the idea and see a worked example

Choose the strongest five from your two private cards and the five shared cards. You may use zero, one or two private cards. Rebuild after each new card; your original hand label can become outdated.

Worked example: You hold Q♠ T♠. The board ends Q♣ 6♠ 2♠ 8♦ 3♥.

Your private cards

Q♠T♠

Shared board

Q♣6♠2♠8♦3♥

The flush missed: only four spades are available. Your best five are Q-Q-T-8-6, a pair of queens. Missing one improvement did not erase the pair.

Read the full stage explanation.

Two pairs on the board

The river is dealt. Use these seven available cards.

Your private cards

9♠9♦

Shared board

K♣K♥Q♦Q♠2♣
Which is your best five-card hand?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Your pocket pair of nines is no longer one of the two pairs in your best five. One nine still supplies the kicker.

A. Kings and queens are a stronger two-pair combination than kings and nines.

B. Yes. Use the two higher board pairs and one nine as the kicker.

C. Only two kings are available. You cannot create a third one.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A shared five-card hand

The button holds the first private hand; the big blind shows the second. Compare both players on this completed board. There are no other players or side pots.

First private hand

2♣2♦

Second private hand (shown)

8♠7♠

Shared board

A♠K♦Q♥J♣T♠
Who has the better five-card hand?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Both players have the same ace-high straight. Suits do not break this tie. Pot division and any odd counter follow the room's procedures; there is no sole winner of this showdown.

A. A pair cannot improve on the board's ace-high straight.

B. Neither private hand improves on the same five-card straight available to both.

C. Yes. Both best hands are A-K-Q-J-T, with zero private cards used.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

One private card matters

Choose from your two private cards and this completed board.

Your private cards

A♥J♦

Shared board

K♥8♥6♥3♥2♣
Which five-card hand can you make?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Five hearts are now available. Count the cards you actually have, rather than carrying the earlier description of a draw into the river.

A. Yes. Your ace of hearts joins four hearts on the board; your jack does not play.

B. Hold'em permits using one private card. It does not require two private cards in the final five.

C. These available ranks do not form five consecutive ranks.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

5. Separate facts and possible hands

Learn the idea and see a worked example

Known cards cannot also be in an opponent's hand. An action is an observation; the hidden cards and how often the opponent takes that action with each hand remain assumptions.

Worked example: You hold A♠ Q♦ and the flop is J♥ 7♣ 2♦. Your opponent checks.

Your private cards

A♠Q♦

Shared board

J♥7♣2♦

The opponent cannot hold A♠ T♦ because you already have that exact ace. A check does not reveal the other cards or prove weakness. Other physically legal hands remain possible.

Read the full stage explanation.

Remove what is already known

Your opponent checks. Consider only which exact private cards are physically possible, not how likely they are.

Your private cards

K♦K♠

Shared board

Q♥8♣2♠
Which opposing hand is still possible?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Remove the five known cards before listing possible opposing holdings. A check does not eliminate the physically possible pair of queens.

A. Your own king of spades cannot also be in the opponent's hand.

B. The queen of hearts is already on the board.

C. Yes. Neither exact card is in your hand or on the board. Possible does not mean likely.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

Read an observed action

Your one opponent checks on this flop. No other information about that player is supplied.

Your private cards

A♥J♠

Shared board

A♣7♣2♦
Which statement is an observed fact?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

A range description separates known cards, legal possibilities and an assumption about frequencies. This scene supplies no measured frequency model.

A. Yes. That describes the action without turning an assumption into a fact.

B. A check does not show the hidden cards or rule out every legal ace.

C. Physical possibility does not supply a frequency for each hand.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

One revealed ending

In one fictional river hand, an opponent bets, is called and reveals a bluff. No previous hands or population data are supplied.

What does this single ending establish?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Record the observation separately from a frequency claim. Reviewing a decision still requires its earlier information and alternatives.

A. One example is not a count of all the player's river bets.

B. Yes. One reveal establishes this ending, not a reliable frequency for future decisions.

C. This ending does not reconstruct the information or alternatives available in other decisions.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

6. Name the purpose of a bet

Learn the idea and see a worked example

A value argument names worse hands that might call. A bluff argument names better hands that might fold. Compare a bet with checking when checking is available, and distinguish a supplied response pattern from evidence about real players.

Worked example: A fictional river model says a worse pair will call your proposed bet. You are trying to get paid by that worse hand.

That is a value argument. It identifies a response from a worse hand. It still does not establish a best bet size or prove betting is better than every alternative.

Read the full stage explanation.

A supplied response

Nothing is owed on the river. In a hypothetical response model, some worse pairs call your proposed bet and no better hand folds. Your stated aim is to get called by those worse pairs.

Which description matches that stated aim?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

The value argument names worse hands that pay. The scene supplies a hypothetical response, not an observed tendency of actual opponents.

A. The supplied model says no better hand folds. That is not the response named in your aim.

B. Yes. The proposed reason is getting paid by worse hands, not a proof of an optimal bet.

C. A hand label alone does not compare checking, sizing or the assumed responses.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

A different desired response

On the river, your draw has missed. Nothing is owed. Your proposed bet is intended to make an opponent fold a better made hand. Whether they will do so often enough is not supplied.

What is the stated purpose?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

You can name the purpose without inventing a fold frequency. This does not establish that the bluff is good or supply a recommended action.

A. Yes. The desired response is a fold from a hand that currently beats yours.

B. The stated target is a better hand folding, not a worse hand calling.

C. A possible fold does not establish its frequency or compare the bet with checking.

Revisit the exact lesson section.

Winning after a bet

In one fictional hand, your river bet makes the opponent fold and you receive the pot. The opponent's hidden cards and response frequencies are not supplied.

Which conclusion is supported by this ending?

Say an answer and its reason before looking at the choices.

Compare your own explanation with the answer panel below.

Explanation and the exact lesson to revisit

Separate an observed result from the reason for an action. A useful review names what response was needed and what was known before the result.

A. The observed fold does not reveal all of the opponent's possible responses.

B. One ending does not supply the comparison with checking or the full set of possible outcomes.

C. Yes. The result is known. The value of the decision against alternatives still needs analysis.

Revisit the exact lesson section.
